newsitem.title: UGANDA: Uganda budgets for most difficult year in a decade.
newsitem.headline: Uganda budgets for most difficult year in a decade.

text.p: Uganda's finance minister said on Thursday that 1997/98 would be the toughest year in a decade as the government grappled with the effects of drought, corruption and civil wars in the East African country.

Presenting his 1997/98 budget to parliament in the capital Kampala, Finance Minister Jehoash Mayanja-Nkangi spoke of "great economic sorrow" and said "we are currently besieged by acts of God" and "greater turbulence ahead".

The 1997/98 budget gave increased funding to President Yoweri Museveni's cherished Universal Primary Education programme that guarantees free primary education for four children per family. It also committed money to improve roads, health care, and agricultural extension and research.
UPE funds rose to 112.5 million shillings ($105,140) from 75 million.
But there were no salary rises for civil servants and ministers surrendered their entitlement to a second official car and travelling first class while on foreign assignments.
The only good news was a rise in manufacturing, foreign investment, and debt relief under a World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF) plan.
Museveni told parliament that corruption and smuggling across Lake Victoria were partly responsible for a slide in growth.
Nkangi announced major currency and trade reforms to make Uganda more competitive and attract more investment and pledged new measures to streamline revenue collection in 1997/98.

He said privatisation of the Uganda Posts & Telecommunications Co was on course as well as that of Uganda Commercial Bank. Part of the two firms would be floated on the Uganda Securities Exchange. The bourse was launched this month but trading has not started.
He saw further streamlining of the banking sector, where current saving rates lie around the three to four percent range compared to lending rates of 22 percent, prohibitive for many Ugandans.
Nkangi put Uganda's overall gross domestic product (GDP) growth at five percent in 1996/97 from 8.2 percent in 1995/96 and forecast modest growth of seven percent in 1997/98.
Nkangi said five percent was critically low for a country used to growth of eight, nine and 10 percent.

He said Uganda's poor fortune was caused by a deterioration in security in the north and southwest on account of civil wars, drought in some areas, coffee and cassava diseases and unusually heavy rains that destroyed crops in western Uganda.

He put underlying inflation that excludes food prices at 1.9 percent in 1996/97 but said overall inflation was up at 11.8 percent from a single digit level in 1995/96. He forecast average inflation at a lower 7.5 percent in 1997/98.

Nkangi said Uganda's total external debt stood at $3.59 billion at end-December 1996 but added that under a World Bank and International Monetary Fund programme of debt relief for heavily indebted poor countries, Uganda would gain a reduction of more than $700 million as early as April 1998.

In 1996/97, Nkangi said he now expected revenues of 773 billion shillings, 43 billion lower than his budget forecast. That compared with expenditures of 1,203 billion, compared to earlier budgetary provisions of 1,172 billion shillings.

Nkangi said he was budgeting for revenues of 840 billion (excluding taxes on government and donor-funded procurements). Of that a total of 829 billion would come from taxes and the balance from appropriations in aid. He put overall government expenditure forecasts at 922 billion shillings.
Nkangi said capital accounts would be liberalised to complete reforms in the foreign currency regime.
The change means residents and non-residents will be free to bring in and take out capital without restriction. Residents will be free to hold foreign accounts and instruments outside the country.
Non-residents will be able to hold foreign exchange accounts in the domestic banking system and instruments denominated in Ugandan shillings, Nkangi added.

In April 1998, bans on the import of beer, sodas and batteries will be terminated. In April 1999, a ban on cigarette imports will be lifted. The bans will be replaced with surcharges that will be phased out within three years.

Nkangi reduced all import duty rates to 20 from 30 percent and said he had harmonised excise duty applicable to imports to 10 percent. The overall import duty will be further reduced to 15 percent in 1998/99 and thereafter to seven percent.
To cushion ordinary Ugandans, Nkangi reduced taxes on petrol, diesel, kerosene, beer, and soft drinks.
($1=1,070 Ugandan shillings)
